summary:
Sakarya is a province in Turkey's Marmara region and stands under the national framework: no Sakarya-specific statute, enforcement programme or local ban concerning transgender visitors is documented in the sources assembled here, and nationwide provisions govern the province's residents and visitors alike.

Turkey has no visa, entry or border rule specific to LGBTQ travellers, so the documented exposure points lie inside the country rather than at the frontier. The visitor-facing document risk is general: foreigners must carry original photo ID at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and warnings of detention for non-compliance. That requirement intersects with identity checks on the street. In August 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women while they were walking, shopping or sitting in cafés in Beyoğlu, held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station and released them after 'General Information Gathering' background checks. Legal experts quoted by bianet argue those checks breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The statutory baseline is permissive on its face. Homosexuality has been decriminalised since 1858 and sex-reassignment surgery has been legal since 1988, but legal gender recognition still requires a court's permission under Civil Code Article 40, with the applicant at least 18, unmarried and holding a medical report from a state-designated hospital. No province-specific rule applies to Sakarya; these provisions govern nationwide.

The most consequential pending measure is the leaked 11th Judicial Package, a 66-page draft amending the Turkish Penal Code, the Civil Code and six other laws, leaked to Turkish media in mid-October 2025 and analysed by Amnesty International in a November 2025 factsheet. Human Rights Watch's release of 29 October 2025 sets out its terms: conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' would carry up to three years' imprisonment, and participation in same-sex ceremonies up to four years. It is the third set of proposed legal amendments targeting LGBTI+ rights during 2025, the earlier two having stalled in Parliament. Whether the package has since passed is unresolved in the sources.

For trans visitors and residents the draft's care and recognition provisions carry the sharpest practical consequences. It would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25 while adding mandatory infertility and multi-evaluation hurdles, imprison providers for up to seven years and patients for up to three, and would raise the minimum age for legal gender recognition procedures from 18 to 25 with further conditions attached. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association object. Amnesty International warns the package would criminalise LGBTI+ people and those advocating for their rights, and would severely restrict or make impossible trans and gender-diverse people's access to gender-affirming healthcare. Those are nationwide proposals applying within every province, Sakarya included.

Hostility is already measurable without the draft. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 records 313 violations over the year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, dominated by 299 detention decisions, 256 taken on the record and 43 off it. Turkish Minute's coverage of the same report counts six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected.

Detainees are held in facilities organised by registered sex rather than gender identity, and Turkish prisons subject LGBTI+ detainees to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare, with no policy or staff training to identify LGBTI+ needs. On 1 December 2025 the transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara; rights groups demanded an independent investigation, and accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers state that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived after prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison only two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. An opposition MP raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025.

Protection machinery is thin. Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity, and no direct discrimination protection for gender identity; the European Commission's 2025 report found legal protection insufficient and out of line with the EU acquis. Hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors must obtain and pay for it privately.
tangentialFactors:
Institutional hostility extends to conscription: the Turkish military bars homosexuals from service and treats homosexuality as a 'psychosexual' illness, a classification with no direct bearing on visitors but one that frames official attitudes toward gender and sexuality.

Public assembly has been constrained by local authorities rather than by a single national statute. Istanbul Pride drew roughly 100,000 participants in 2013 and 2014 before the 2015 to 2018 parades were banned by local authorities. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the year, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Policing asymmetry is documented at case level. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy by a 17-year-old; the attacker was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, which activists describe as evidence of a state hate policy. The Erdoğan government has repeatedly used 'the family' and 'public morals' framing to legitimise stigmatisation, and the reform package sits within a broader authoritarian drift.

The legislative sequence matters for expectations: two earlier amendment packages targeting LGBTI+ rights stalled in Parliament during 2025 before the October leak, so a draft's existence is not itself a reliable predictor of enactment.

outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the leaked 11th Judicial Package has been enacted, amended or abandoned since the October 2025 leak and the November 2025 Amnesty International factsheet is unresolved in the sources; no post-November legislative record is available here.

No source in this inventory records any Sakarya-specific policing practice, local by-law, municipal ban or provincial enforcement programme affecting transgender visitors. The absence of such material is a limit of the sources assembled, not a finding that none exists.

The inventory contains no entry, visa or residence-permit material specific to Sakarya, and no reporting on how identity documents are handled at Sakarya's own transit checkpoints; the ID and checkpoint rules cited here are national and drawn from other provinces.

Whether court permission under Civil Code Article 40 has been granted or refused at any particular rate in Sakarya is not sourced, and the practical processing time for such petitions in the province is unknown.
